The Pallid bat Antrozous pallidus is a medium-sized vespertilionid native to arid and semi-arid regions of western North America. Neonates are notably small, with a birth mass of just 3.1 grams [Wwb = 3.1 grams], a value that reflects the altricial state of the newborn pup. This initial size is modest compared to the ultimate adult body mass, which reaches approximately 20.8 grams [Wwi = approximately 20.8 grams] in reproductively active individuals, though field records indicate a broader range of 14 to 25 grams across different populations. Reproductive activity in this species is tightly linked to seasonal temperatures; when females are maintained under controlled conditions at a steady 34 °C [T = 34 °C], the time from copulation to parturition, or gestation time, lasts precisely 62 days [tg = 62 days]. This relatively extended gestation is striking for a mammal of this body size and likely reflects the energetic constraints imposed by a diet of large, hard-bodied arthropods such as scorpions and beetles.

Following parturition, the dependency period of the nursing pup is brief yet critical. The weaning age, marking the end of lactation and the onset of solid food consumption, occurs at 50 days after birth [tx = 50 days after birth] when the young are maintained at 34 °C [T = 34 °C]. This rapid transition to nutritional independence is characteristic of many insectivorous bats, which must acquire foraging skills quickly to survive. The suckling juvenile relies entirely on maternal milk during the first several weeks, a period during which the mother undertakes nightly foraging bouts to sustain her own energy balance while provisioning the pup. The development of flight and echolocation capabilities accelerates around the time of weaning, allowing the juvenile to begin capturing prey on its own by approximately two months of age. This early independence is essential in the seasonal environments Pallid bats occupy, where prey availability peaks during the warm summer months and declines rapidly with the onset of cooler autumn weather.

Sexual maturation in Antrozous pallidus proceeds relatively slowly for a bat of its size. The age at which individuals attain puberty, defined by the onset of spermatogenesis in males and first ovulation in females, is estimated to occur at 365 days since birth [tp = 365 days since birth] when the animals are held at a constant 34 °C [T = 34 °C]. This interval corresponds to roughly one full calendar year, meaning that young born in the late spring typically become reproductively competent by the following breeding season. The delay reflects the substantial energetic investment required to reach the adult body mass of 20.8 grams [Wwi = 20.8 grams] and to complete the neurological and skeletal development necessary for effective flight and hunting. In natural populations, this timing is synchronized by photoperiod and temperature cues, ensuring that first mating opportunities coincide with periods of high insect abundance.

Lifespan data for Pallid bats come primarily from field-based mark-recapture studies and captive observations. The maximum recorded longevity for individuals living under natural conditions is approximately 5,402 days [am = approximately 5,402 days] when measured at an ambient temperature of 10 °C [T = 10 °C], a value that corresponds to roughly 14.8 years. This considerable lifespan is typical for vespertilionid bats, which are known for their slow life-history pace and high survival rates relative to similarly sized terrestrial mammals. The low ambient temperature in this measurement reflects the hibernation torpor that individuals experience during winter months, a state that dramatically reduces metabolic expenditure and is thought to contribute to the species' extended longevity. In contrast, captive individuals maintained under warmer, stable conditions may experience different aging trajectories, though comparative data remain sparse.

Reproductive output in Antrozous pallidus is constrained by the species' annual cycle and the energetic demands of lactation. Females typically produce a single litter each year, with a maximum reproductive rate characterized by a single pup per litter [N_R_i = single pup per litter] and a frequency of one litter annually [F_R_i = one litter annually]. At a body temperature of 34 °C [T = 34 °C], this translates to a maximum rate of just over two pups every three years per female. The small litter size, a common trait among bats, is offset by high juvenile survival and the extended lifespan of the adult. Maternity colonies, which can number in the hundreds, provide a thermal environment that supports the elevated body temperatures required for gestation and lactation. Comparisons with other vespertilionids of similar body mass suggest that this conservative reproductive strategy is linked to the species' reliance on unpredictable prey resources, where a single, well-provisioned offspring has a higher survival probability than multiple, underdeveloped littermates.
